newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Europe pressures Sweden on ERM issue.
newsitem.headline: Europe pressures Sweden on ERM issue.

text.p: Sweden's idiosyncratic stance on the qualifications for membership of the EMU currency union risks putting the country at loggerheads with the rest of Europe, Europe's top central bankers say.
Sweden insists that currency stability, not membership of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM), is the key factor for participation in the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
But Sweden needs to think again, according to key players who spoke to Swedish journalists during a visit of central bankers and finance ministries in the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium.
Europe's core countries demand that Sweden fulfils the exchange rate criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty if the crown is to be allowed entry into the single European currency.

"The German government has no other choice than to demand a strict and tight interpretation," Juergen Stark, state secretary at the German finance department and German representative on the EU's monetary committee, told Reuters.
Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer drew the same conclusion.
"The treaty is clear on this point, membership in ERM is a condition," Tietmeyer told Swedish reporters in Brussels.
A strict intepretation of the treaty could mean it's all over for Sweden.
The Maastricht Treaty says a currency must be pegged to ERM for at least two years before the state or government heads decide which countries have met the criteria for EMU entry.
"This must be valid for at least two years before the decision is taken in the spring of 1998 on which countries will take part," said Stark.
However he said there was still some room for manoeuvre.
A point of view which has been expressed by many is that ERM participation is not only about stability. It also concerns finding a suitable central rate for the crown.
"ERM has two elements, the one is currency stability, the other is the definition of parity," said Tietmeyer.
Belgian central bank chief Alfons Verplaetse told Reuters the central Riksbank would need to determine a value for the crown, if only unilaterally.
Asked how he viewed the Swedish Riksbank's opinion that it can intervene in the currency market in order to keep the crown stable, Verplaetse said:
"This solution I personally can live with but only if the Riksbank declares a parity level for the crown," he said.
Some central bank sources said Sweden's belief that its parliament would decide on membership of the single currency had come as a surprise to EU decision-makers.

"I am astonished. There is no one to make a decision on how to interpret the Maastricht Treaty and whether or not one is fulfilling the convergence criteria," said a central bank representative, who declined to be identified.
The only countries given the choice under the treaty are Britain and Denmark. Swedish reference to a protocol note, which it claims gives parliament the right to vote on the issue, doesn't count.
The emerging picture is of Sweden seeking to obtain what it did not get in negotiations ahead of EU entry - the ability to say no to the single currency.
How will the Swedish government react to this pressure from the rest of Europe? Prime Minister Goran Persson will not be imposed upon.
"Hans Tietmeyer has nothing to say about this (Sweden's EMU policy)," Persson told journalists at the weekend.
